items.body: Expanding rather than merging the recognized individual styles of each, Fictions results in a chronostatic set of pieces with error honored as a hidden intention (see Eno’s Oblique Strategies) via analog processes, while holding to melodic virtues and economy of means. Languorous veiled melodies choreographed into an immersive suite Fictions by Lamasz & Grandbruit   Following release in early July, Fictions, somewhat mirroring its own dynamic, has taken time to reach peak resonance, creeping via auditory channels into psychoactive life, effectively bringing together the defining elements of each of Lamasz and Grandbruit into a single body of work. The return to Past Inside the Present of Pierre Luc (Lamasz) and Francis Tremblay (Grandbruit) with this collaboration comes on the back of four solo releases across the label: Fictions draws on Nature Morte (2020) and Broderie (2021) in tape loop-driven nature, Ruptures (2020) and Ville inerte (2021) in use of stratified guitar and environmental sound, common ground found in manicured noise, overall ambience and recursive habit. The brothers allow a gradual evolution, pieces looping into processed guitar-smeared harmonic tracts, tape hiss effectively taking on an active compositional role transcending background color. Expanding rather than merging the recognized individual styles of each, Fictions results in a chronostatic set of pieces with error honored as a hidden intention (see Eno’s Oblique Strategies) via analog processes, while holding to melodic virtues and economy of means. Fictions, then, adds to both artists’ growing back catalog, with languorous veiled melodies choreographed into an immersive suite with an emotional heft matching its timbral resonance. RIYL Chihei Hatakeyama, Rafael Anton Irisarri and artists in adjacent zones. items.body: Melodic gestures emerge from drone surrounds—ground to figure, dissolving into field—drawing you in from perception’s margins, receding just as they seem to have settled. A platform to explore themes of presence, absence, removal and acceptance Disappear in Silent Ways by Halftribe   At the intersection of ambient, drone and environmental sound you’ll find Halftribe. His return to Dronarivm, Disappear in Silent Ways, comes in colors at once luminous and blurred, with a captivating ambi[val]ence, evoking a sense of moments presenting with past inside. Evanescence. This is achieved partly via a keen melodic sensibility with soft analog-y synths, field captures and odd voice fragments crafted into tone poems at once expansive and intimate. A form of minimalism runs through DiSW, manifest not in ideological stance but simple compositional practice; Ryan Bissett eschews the impulse for new entries to the sound stage for letting sounds evolve, adding color to broader canvas before letting in other elements. Sounds recede then return, revenant—a vague sense of movement over overt development; a soft ebb-flow dynamic, harmonic shifts emerging to color tenor, drones privileging depth over density, minute tonal shifts reframing space around and within. Melodic gestures emerge from drone surrounds—ground to figure, dissolving into field—drawing you in from perception’s margins, receding just as they seem to have settled. A site of refuge found after disappearing :: “Listen,” bids us attend to our environs, with its leitmotif ‘what we listen to is constantly feeding us’ adjuring mindfulness of what we let in. Field recordings bring in the natural world, as on “Dusk,” mixing layered drones with rainfall, evoking crepuscular horizons in day-night transition, inner-outer boundaries dissolved; or “Sanctuary,” pointing to a site of refuge found after disappearing; its oneiric mood feeds into “Yearn,” water flow enhancing a sense of peace through nature connection. “Windfall” shifts focus from water, distant whispers suggesting a field with grass and trees windblown, light filtering through branches to slow cloud drift. The title track brings an interlude of release, with birdsong and babbling before “Everything Comes to an End” leaves us with… that sense of evanescence. Following For the Summer, or Forever (2018) and Elegant, Golden (2022), Dronarivm has provided Halftribe with a platform to explore themes of presence, absence, removal and acceptance. The artist’s stamp, though, is more outline than full imprint, DiSW not looking to thematic statement so much as documenting the resonance of a feeling, in all its contours. items.body: Parissior is a Spanish project founded by DJ and producer Jesu Aparicio. With “Human Control”, he releases his debut album, featuring ten tracks (although the vinyl edition contains only eight). While several EPs were released previously, this album consists entirely of new material, exploring themes such as digital identity, illusion, authenticity, and human imperfection. Musically, this translates into a very solid mix of Dark-Techno and EBM. The basslines sound menacing and pure EBM, while the kicks reveal clear Techno influences. There are also a few additional influences, such as Acid sequences, as well as some delightful old-school Techno elements that remind me of the Frankfurt scene of the 1990s. The way everything is put together sounds intelligent and, naturally, highly dancefloor-oriented. There are also some vocals worth mentioning, including a track featuring guest vocalist Jorge Tornin, although the vocals are not necessarily the most striking aspect of the album. “Human Control” is a very strong release that delivers a perfect blend of nostalgic moments and a more contemporary sound, in which Dark-Techno and EBM are inseparable and form a powerful cocktail. An album you absolutely must discover! (Rating:8½). Listen to “Eco Machines”: Eco Machines by Parissior About Parissior Parissior is the alias of Spanish DJ and producer Jesu Aparicio. He has released singles and EPs since at least 2016, including “Could I Drown In Your Desire” and “Dance To The Groove” (Spa In Disco), followed by “Let Them Dance” (Hot Digits Music, 2017) and further EPs and compilation appearances for Golden Soul Records. From “Back To Earth” (2020) onward he has worked mainly with the Espacio Cielo label, releasing further singles, EPs and compilation tracks including “Battle Cry” (2021), “Raver In The Booth” and “Full of Stars” (2023), and the Skylax release “Antennae” (2024). “Human Control” is his first full-length album.

items.body: Norvik, aka Gabriel Chan, is a composer from Hong Kong. His new album, Echo Theory, takes into consideration our place in the Universe, from the smallest flower to the biggest star. Although we are tiny, beautiful things often come in small packages, and size doesn’t diminish our place or importance in the grand scheme of things: we are special, precious, breathing into the cosmic wonder of the Universe and sharing in its majesty, a part of a chapter in its ongoing story. As Norvik says, ‘there is value to being humbled’, and the piano melodies are enraptured by the space in which we live. Atoms coalesce, eventually forming the biggest stars and growing like seeds to forge a blossoming Galaxy, of which there are billions and counting; where stars hang like stationary snowflakes, pinned to unending black. Chan’s piano melodies are just as precious. Each one lights up like a star, and each one inhabits a lonely world. The ambient atmosphere pulls the piano into an orbit where it’s free to turn and swirl; a radiant ballet, and without the restrictive law of gravity to shackle it. The surrounding atmosphere, brought about by a vacuum of synth and a set of chiming electronics which flirt with new age music, is a dark expanse over which the piano may play. Space is the ultimate playground, and in the piano, Chan adds a twinkle of colour, creating splashes of light which predate time, returning to the dawn of starlight and the Big Bang itself. At other times, such as ‘Sturmfrei’, a celestial ambient comes to take over, gleaming with a sci-fi sheen, like something from Halo. ‘Hiraeth’ is equally stunning, and the closing strings provide a comforting end. Exceptionally warm and delivered from the heart despite a pursuit of the monolithic, Chan’s music lights up the world and beyond. What is life without emotion, and living without loving? Chan’s music is emotional and mega in scale, but there’s a beautiful intimacy, too. The Universe may be vast beyond all measure, but the heart’s capacity for love is infinite, no matter how small its cage, aka, the body. Everything has a place, regardless of size. Inklings turn into dreams. Thousand-mile journeys begin with a single step. A butterfly spreads her wings in Asia and a hurricane sweeps through Florida. Everything and everyone starts somewhere, and there’s infinite value in that. There’s also something comforting in being so little; Earth’s children wrapped up in the spiral arms of the Milky Way, a mother to a child. www.norvik.bandcamp.com

items.body: (You are here) Somewhere With his latest work, (You are here) Somewhere, part of a new flurry of releases on Impulsive Habitat, Bruno Duplant seems to have given us an aural adaptation of Marc Augé’s famous book Non-Places: Introduction to an Anthropology of Supermodernity (1995)… In his essay, Augé theorized the idea of the “non-place, the ambivalent space that has none of the familiar attributes of place and which incites no sense of belonging.” What he investigated, were not only those generic spaces necessary to the accelerated circulation of goods and people, such as airports and bus terminals, but also those anonymous “rest and recreation” environments such as chain hotels and shopping malls, which can be found anywhere in the globalised world. This idea is certainly not new and has been looked at before. I am thinking of Simon Whetham’s Mall Muzac (Unfathomless, 2011), for instance, where Whetham captured recordings in The Mall, Broadmead, Bristol. And yet, Duplant’s album is still an effective exercise in sonic dislocation, a timely reminder of the increasingly depersonalized landscape, the ever increasing gentrification of many urban centers the world over, is bringing about. The French composer and sound artist makes no concessions, collecting “sounds from everywhere. From inside & outside” and offers them raw, with no treatment. The result is both familiar and destabilizing. I found myself trying to latch on to any recognizable sounds, such as snippets of conversation in languages that seemed identifiable, in order to give some concrete domesticity to this alienating “Somewhere”. Ultimately, the sonic environment captured by Dupont is the aural equivalent of stock images from picture libraries, too mundane and immediately accessible to have any real meaning. It is only valid as a sort of shortcut to suggest transit and idleness. Snatches of Excerpts of baroque music, for instance, were never going to act as a geographical compass. There is no definite indication of any timeframe either. The sound of what could be crickets introduces a seasonal marker, but the uncertainty of whether this might belong to an interior space quickly transforms it into a mechanical buzz. Birdsongs merges with a busy fuzziness punctuated by beeps that subverts any pastoral suggestion. And yet, I found myself back in the countryside with more cricket song. An unedited recurring mobile phone interference suggests that the kind of aural anthropology of daily life pursued by Duplant cannot be approached without taking into account the pervasive connectivity we are trapped in. The irony being that there is nothing here I could connect with. Or rather, I could connect with so much, as to make the whole exercise meaningless. By the time I could distinctly detect a few words of French spoken towards the end of the second part, I was beyond caring, even though, finding out where I was supposed to be, should never have been the goal of this listening experience. This “Somewhere” is not somewhere I long to spend time in. But sometimes it is important to be reminded of this. (You are here) Somewhere by Bruno Duplant is available as a free download on Impulsive Habitat. www.impulsivehabitat.com

items._cn_summary: Bruno Duplant的专辑《(You are here) Somewhere》以田野录音为核心手法，作者采集自"各处"的内外声音，不做任何处理地直接呈现给听众。评论将这张作品与法国人类学家Marc Augé的"非地方"理论并置，探讨全球化背景下机场、商场等匿名空间所带来的疏离感。整张专辑刻意制造声音的错位与去人格化体验：听众试图抓住可辨识的语言片段或环境声来定位自身，却发现这些声音如同图库素材般平庸而即时，缺乏深意。评论特别提到巴洛克音乐片段未能充当地理坐标，蟋蟀声在内外空间之间模糊切换，未编辑的手机干扰噪音暗示当代人无处逃遁的连接状态，而这种无处连接本身又构成了悖论。评论在末尾截断，未完结。

items.body:
After the OĽUN album I reviewed enthusiastically a while back, here’s the next project, again motivated and led by violinist/fiddler/composer Ján Kružliak Jr., continuing the rapprochement, indeed embrace, between Slovakia’s traditional music and its classical music. This time it reconnects the works of classical composers who were inspired by and drew on village musics with those traditional sources and styles.
Three ensembles are involved: the Spectrum Quartett led by Kru�liak with two violins, viola and cello; Nogaband, the traditional-style quartet of fiddles, contra (chording viola) and bass that’s led by fiddler and singer Michal Noga; and the female vocal group Ulijanky, plus guest singer Simona Hulejov�.
The majority of the tracks are interpretations of works by Slovak composer Eugen Suchon (1908-1993), with others from fellow-Slovaks Ilja Zeljenka (1932-2007) and Alexander Moyzes (1906-1984), and Hungarian B�la Bart�k (1881-1945) who did a lot of his very detailed collecting of folk music in Slovakia.
In each case the sources - musicians and locations in villages across Slovakia - are credited in the notes, and these arrangements and performances reconnect with the energy and traditional vocal sound of those sources.
In no way is this an orchestra-smoothed thing; this is gutsy, brilliantly played and sung music with all the spirit, skill and technique of traditional music, from players and singers who deeply understand and inhabit it. It’s a glorious piece of work, music to luxuriate in. There’s too much richness to begin to detail, but here’s a dip into a few moments to give the flavor. The tracks all have very long titles detailing their sources, so for brevity’s sake I’ll just give track numbers.

items.body: "There is no such thing as a stranger�s children." - old Ukrainian saying I�ve long been affected, indeed somewhat obsessed, by what�s happening in Ukraine, partly because of one of my favorite bands, DakhaBrakha. I went to Kyiv to see them at the time of the Maidan protests, just after the shooting by snipers of over a hundred protesters. I intentionally didn�t read this album�s booklet notes before listening, so that I could react to it without sympathetic pre-judgement, just as music. It�s strong musically and vocally by any standards, Ukrainian or otherwise. When I did then turn to the notes that translate and explain the songs, I had that rare experience, for me, of becoming moist-eyed. The songs are a mix of traditional and original. They are focused on the abduction by Russia of about 20,000 Ukrainian children who have been taken from their parents in Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine and sent to Russia, in an attempt to turn them into haters of their native land and people. It�s a heinous war crime. Marichka is a Ukrainian-Canadian singer who moves between Canada and her homeland. For this album she�s gathered two groups of musicians, one in each country. Both ensembles contribute vocals and instrumentation, mostly bowed strings, plus some bandura and piano. The group in Ukraine includes Lisa from the destroyed and invaded city of Mariupol, playing a solo on double ocarina; at 16 she was one of the stolen children but managed to return to Ukraine. Daughters of Donbas � co-led by Marichka and singer/bandurist Alina Kuzma, who shares the lead vocal role � is an all-female ensemble in Canada that tours performing these songs. �Foreign Land� is a reworking of a traditional song about the young girls who were sent away to work in foreign households - Marichka�s grandmother was one of these - that can also be taken to refer to the plight of today�s stolen children. The translation goes: A mother packed up her daughter To leave for a strange land To a strange land with strange people Oh, who will pity you, my daughter? Those who will beat me will pity me I'll never again live with you, my mother When, my daughter, should I expect you to come home? When the grass in the garden grows, my mother The grass grew and grew and began to dry The mother was waiting for her daughter to return, and began to cry Did you hear, my mother, how I came to you? How I flew as a bird above your window? How I cooed like a dove? If, my daughter, I could hear you I would open all the doors and windows To let you fly in Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Alina Kuzma, Zo� Santo As befits the song, Marichka�s vocal here is gentle. But in the second track, �Rusalka,� with Alina Kuzma taking the lead vocals, things turn harsh and fierce. A rusalka is a mythical creature, a nature spirit of fields, forest and rivers, that features in traditional ritual songs. The melody of this one is by Zo� Santo and Kuzma, with lyrics drawing on tradition and the composition of Santo and 19thC Ukrainian poet and folklorist Taras Shevchenko. An ominous double-bass drone, chunking strings, a slithering vocal that moves into sections of white-voice fast recitative and expands into a soaring wild cry. The lyrics are very dark, perhaps evoking the hell of the front line: Home a hell of old growth stumps Marsh a mud of memories Don�t get bogged down in these parts Your kind won�t last a day in here While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. A rusalka sat on a white birch, rusalky asked girls for shirts. Long fingers and nails so sharp Tongue forked round serrated teeth Moss grows down beneath her parts Weeds braided from ear to ear While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. �Girls, my friends, give me your shirts. Though I�m thin, give me a thin one.� Here live us the backless ones Many voices of dead sons You are right to quake in fear Send your sinful children here �Who Am I� is a plea of separation and disorientation, the pain and confusion of an abducted child, contrasting �the human in me� and �the creature in me,� like an internalized riddle-song, with the refrain, in English: Who am I for you? Who am I for me? Do you know me? Really know me? �Enchantress,� passionately sung by Kuzma to her own bandura accompaniment, a girl�s lament of the loss of her brave love taken from her by the enchantress, who is an allegory of war, is based on a traditional song and uses that style of melody and lyrics, �Riddle,� sung by Marichka, reworks a traditional riddle song to be the riddles told by the grandfather of a child, 12-year-old Kira from Mariupol, who experienced the death of her father and her abduction to Russia. Her grandfather tracked her down, and brought her back, traumatized, and asked her riddles - as the notes say �to jog her memory, and remind her who she was, where her home was, and of her family�s love for her.� Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �4.5.0� is a military expression for �all�s well� or �all is quiet.� The song is a message, as from a mother, to a stolen child. Marichka�s voice is cherishing: Remember this: I am with you, I am here Don't give up, I'm with you. Don't give up, I'm with you Your hope is my weapon Don't be sad, I'm with you 4.5.0. will be again �breaking into a tearing howl: And when the world's axis breaks When the sky folds like a parchment Out of nowhere her words will come� �and back to fragile reassurance �It's all right, I'm here, I'm here� "Lullaby," based on a traditional lullaby, sung by Alina Kuzma to accompaniment by her bandura and Zo� Santo's viola, starts in gentle lullaby style, but moves to a lament; it's for the stolen children and those who, as the notes put it, 'have been stolen for ever.' Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �Remember, I Believe in You� is a powerful piece of harmonizing vocals and slithering strings. Here�s the story it�s based on: Yevhen lived in Mariupol with his three young children. During the siege they lived in a basement bomb shelter for months. One day, Russian soldiers entered their bomb shelter. Yevhen was taken to a filtration camp and separated from his children who were all taken to a hospital and then to Russian summer �camp�. In the filtration camp Yevhen was brutally tortured and forced to sleep standing on one leg. He tried to fall asleep, whispering prayers for his children: �Everything will be fine, I believe in you.� After his release he walked 30 kilometers to the place where his children had been taken but it was too late. They had already been sent to Moscow. Yevhen learned of this after receiving a text from one of his children who had found an unattended device. He traveled thousands of kilometers, crossed the borders of three countries, endured checks, interrogations and danger to reach Moscow and take his children home. All those days he tirelessly repeated to himself, �I believe in myself, I believe in my kids. Everything will be good.� �Another Heaven,� sung by Marichka with the ensemble in Ukraine, is inspired by another heart-rending story: Ilya was 9 years old when his mother was killed by a rocket strike right in front of him. He was taken to a hospital in occupied Donetsk, where 15 pieces of shrapnel were removed from his body without anesthesia. After he appeared in a report on Russian television, Ilya�s grandmother learned his location. She managed to bring her grandson to Kyiv, where he lives now, experiencing missile attacks every night. At age 11, he says that it is up to everyone to fight enemies, to protect other cities, and to build another heaven, where your home will not be destroyed. In 2014, during the Kyiv Maidan protests, Marichka wrote and performed �Red Boots Tango,� using a melody she�d put to a poem by Taras Shevchenko. For this album she sings it again in Ukraine, with the ensemble there adding swirling, classic tango-style strings. Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, BanduraGirl The final track on the album is a solo, recorded in Kyiv, by Anastasiya Voytyuk, accompanying herself on the older, simpler form of bandura that was used by kobzars to accompany epic poetry, and also on the nowadays more well-known big, heavy form developed from it in Soviet times that was made mainly in the piano factory at Chernihiv. Her song, �Soon I Will Be Back,� is based on a poem by novelist, journalist and war crime researcher Victoria Amelia, who was killed in 2023, in the city of Kramatorsk in Donbas, by a Russian rocket. Find the artist online. Further reading: Otava Yo - Do You Love (Review) Sofia Rei - Umbral (Review)

items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s by Various Artists In general, what�s on offer here, like Volume 1, was recorded at Radio Sao Tom� e Principe (RSTP), often taped in the courtyard outside at night, and released on cassette or occasionally, vinyl. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. And Bongo Joe, who have also released two volumes featuring the above mentioned Africa Negra, have given this music the treatment it deserves, with extensive notes on the country�s history, vintage photographs, and band discographies. items.body: A confession to begin: I�ve been a fan of Alison Cotton�s music for quite a while, so the announcement of a new album definitely brought me a frisson of delight. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The centerpiece, however, is �Sprigs of Heather,� with an opening that recalls medieval sacred music that becomes a simple, slowly cascading, piano-led melody. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. items.body: Those of us who have been digging into Analog Africa�s increasingly formidable releases over the last two decades are well aware of the massive amount of raw, vodun-based Sato and Sakpata-derived funk the label has issued by Benin�s most prolific 1970s-era band, the Orchestre Poly-Ritmo. AA has dropped no fewer than 3 compilations of their heaviest material, as well as a reissue of the band�s first LP, in an effort to give them the international status they deserve. That being said, what might be different about this collection of their music? And who is Antoine Dougb�? Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa As it turns out, Dougb� was a song-conjurer whose mode of musical transfer was slapping his legs in a rhythm known as Cavacha, a groove created by drummer Belobi Meridjo, who was inspired by a train cadence that he worked into a pattern that ultimately spread like a 21st century California wildfire throughout Congolese pop music in the mid-1970s. Dougb�, known as the �Devil�s Prime Minister,� was also a practitioner of vodun who inspired fear in any musician he felt was unsuited to play his music, which is how he landed on working exclusively Poly-Ritmo, as he felt they could nail what he wanted in ways other bands couldn�t. His recording career was brief - 3 albums and a few singles - but as this collection shows, it was potent. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa Because of the era from which this music dates, it�s not surprising that the recording and instrument tones have changed - the guitars have a plastic sheen and synthesizers appear- even if the music remains rooted in the 1970s. Perhaps the influence of the Cuban son is more apparent here than on other Poly-Ritmo collections, especially in the collection�s initial offerings. And yes, Congolese rumba, then shaking all of sub-Saharan Africa to its knees, is present too. �Ma Won Min Towe Leo� is one example. Opening with a bed of synthesizers, the shimmering guitars, tinny, seemingly squeezed dry by the 80s themselves, lock in over relentless high-hat-focused grooves. The guitars finally start firing in different directions midway through, before that synth weaves back in, forming a bed underneath it all. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa �We Tayi Sin Assi Tche� is much more overtly Cuban. With its insistent cowbell, classic, nasal vocal call and response, and tight, repeated guitar figures, its debt to mid-twentieth century Afro-Cuban sons is transparent. Another track, �Djomido Ma Dougbe Tche� rides a groove reminiscent of 70�s-era Franco classic �Liberte.� The pulse is relentless, and the guitar solo repeats a tight repetition of a few notes, driving listeners to ecstasy all the while. However, none of this music is a mere copy of its influences; rather, like so much potent pop coming from the continent at the time, it is a swirl of major influences rendered by local rhythms and vocal phrasing to give it specific identity, in this case, to Benin. Dougb�s musical role on this collection is a bit murky. One of his three albums has a photo of him, fully mic�d behind a collection of hand drums, so perhaps he served as a percussionist/vocalist; this release never explains. He wasn�t a songwriter in the traditional sense. It seems he was more of an instigator and arranger, but his thumbprint was apparently heavy enough to warrant his name on the records he was involved with. Whatever the case, in his brief run as a recording artist, he and Poly-Ritmo produced a handful of driving, Cavacha-inspired grooves that can still wear holes in club floors. items.body: After the extra-terrestial explorations of Eventyrferd , the previous album from Norway's Camilla Hole Trio, in which sci-fi synth sounds were married with traditional material, their latest release Langs is rather more earthbound. But the quest to look beyond their own country's folk music continues. Camilla Hole's main instrument being the soprano sax, the influence of jazz is unsurprising and this is evident in the opening track �Springleik,� signifying a tune used to accompany the springleik dance from the west of Norway. Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. But characteristically for this trio, in which assigned roles are never clearly defined or adhered to, things soon start to move around, with Kalman taking up the melody on his bass, playing the melody in unison with Hole, while Nesheim opens things out further rhythmically. As the whole piece takes on a much more improvisatory feel, Hole plays the melody one more time as things draw to a close. Langs by Camilla Hole Trio

items.body: Kommission Z80 is a Swedish duo that, following a debut album released on Electric Underground Records, is now self-releasing its second opus. I don’t recall ever hearing anything by them before, but these 13 tracks provide a clear picture of the duo’s musical identity. Their primary influences clearly lie within the realm of old-school EBM—specifically the kind of EBM characterized by thoughtful composition and well-crafted arrangements. The vocals, and indeed some of the tracks, remind me somewhat of Portion Control, while other songs reveal traces of Skinny Puppy’s influence. One track even feels like a nod to Front 242. It should be noted that these are all bands with highly distinctive sounds and complex structures. Kommission Z80 doesn’t quite reach that level yet; they would benefit from improving some technical aspects, particularly the mixing and recording. Nevertheless, there is undeniable potential here. Several strong tracks are waiting to be discovered, and the latter part of the album, in particular, features some very cool songs. Kommission Z80 is a name that true EBM enthusiasts should remember. (Rating:7). Listen to “Here Comes The Consequences”: Here Comes The Consequences by Kommission Z80 About Kommission Z80 Kommission Z80 is a Swedish duo from Borås formed by Erik Holmberg and Fredrich Legnemark, working in an old-school EBM style. The project’s debut single “Empire” arrived in 2024 through Electric Underground Records, followed by the debut album “Hegemony” and the “Reasonable Conclusions” EP in 2025. “Sic Semper Tyrannis” is the duo’s self-released 2026 follow-up.

items.body: Are we better off alone Will I come into my own Are we better off alone Being understood by someone is a comfort until the relationship ends and their imagined opinion starts conducting an inspection of everything wrong with you. Boy Harsher’s Faulty inhabits that uncomfortable interval between asking to be wanted and wondering what that wanting has cost. Jae Matthews sings as though the verdict may already be in, while Augustus Muller gives her doubts enough room to move. The question of being better off alone becomes something to turn over on the dancefloor, where thinking clearly has always been optional. The song accompanies the release of Get Mean, out now following its September 18 arrival through Atlantic Records. Their first album since 2022’s The Runner, the twelve-track record follows the end of Matthews and Muller’s romantic relationship in early 2024, after a period of family loss, personal upheaval, and creative uncertainty. Continuing the band meant finding a way to work together while the terms of their lives were changing. That makes the tenderness of Faulty particularly affecting: the people making this music understand how complicated its questions can become. A kicking beat, busy hi-hats, and quivering synths set Faulty in motion. Its dark disco rhythm has some of Careful’s physical insistence, softened by broad synth pads and little descending electronic notes that drop through the arrangement with a rounded, almost playful boop. When the beat pauses to breathe, the synths take on a Vangelis-like warble, briefly opening the song into something more spacious and cinematic. The rhythm returns beneath a lead synth that bends up and down in pitch, while Matthews keeps her voice hushed and close, breathing the words with a tenderness that borders on resignation. The lyrics put affection and self-assessment in an uncomfortable room together. Asking whether she is faulty gives another person the power to diagnose her; asking whether she will come into her own begins to take some of that power back. Repetition keeps either possibility from becoming a settled conclusion. Matthews sounds caught between wanting to be held and recognizing how much of herself might be waiting outside the relationship. Directed by Boy Harsher and shot on 35mm with cinematography by Owen Smith-Clark, the final video in the Get Mean series returns to a room lined in brown wood paneling. A television glows blue on a black stand, a small fan sits by the window, and a microphone cable trails across the carpet. Against that ordinary setting, the changing cast look dressed for entirely different evenings: a white cowboy hat, metallic bodysuits, striped knitwear, black boots. Each person seems to have brought a private version of the same bad night. The camera moves from fixed views of the room into close-ups of faces, hands, and bodies moving past one another. People share the frame, lean together, or briefly touch, but proximity never quite settles the question in the chorus. There is a lovely awkwardness to it: the self-consciousness of dancing at home, followed by the sudden absorption of forgetting you are being watched. By the end, the people have gone and the television is still there. The room has held all that feeling without offering anyone an answer. Watch the video for Faulty below: Across Get Mean, the effort to keep going takes several musical forms. Writing began to move again when Matthews took to the road, travelling through West Texas, the Pacific Northwest, and South Florida. The album was eventually recorded in eight locations across the United States, Mexico, and Italy, its unsettled circumstances allowing new sounds and approaches into the duo’s work. Matthews describes it as “what I had to give during the most extreme period of my life.” The three singles we covered ahead of its release made clear how much that offering could contain. The first indication came with Jeans, released in June. Its springy guitar figure and bubbling electronics brought a new wave directness to Boy Harsher, with a steel-slide twang giving the song a western accent. Our earlier comparison to the Pretenders still fits the way Matthews’ cool delivery rides that guitar, while the buoyancy also suggests Muller’s work in Safe Mind. Beneath the cheek is a sharp little study of ambition: the dream of escaping a small town, the dream of becoming somebody, and the possibility of ending up selling an image of freedom by the pair. The band’s latex line-dancing video, conceived with Robert Palmer’s Addicted to Love in mind, makes that collision between aspiration, performance, and merchandise deliciously literal. Hard Beat, unveiled alongside July’s album announcement, tightens the pressure around a repeating bass-synth figure and an unrelenting kick. As we noted then, there is something of Depeche Mode’s Behind the Wheel in its meeting of motion, desire, and surrendered control. Matthews moves between confession and invitation while the rhythm keeps pushing ahead. Its video makes those exchanges physical through an elaborate leg brace, a Cadillac, and a handheld camcorder, drawing medical hardware, automotive controls, and the invasive act of filming into the same uneasy visual language. Within the album, the track preserves the severe club momentum that has long served Boy Harsher so well, giving the softer and more openly melodic songs something solid to push against. August’s Tough Luck (When You Don’t Call) puts a warmer arrangement around the indignity of waiting for someone to remember you exist. A brisk new wave beat, rounded bass, bright keyboards, and short bursts of distorted guitar carry Matthews’ unhappy drawl toward the sort of pop chorus that can make despair briefly feel sociable. Her insistence that she is okay sounds increasingly like something she needs to practice. Our earlier review followed that idea into the lyric video, where yellow karaoke lettering crosses the blue screen of a CRT television. Created with vintage video equipment by Sean McGuirk and shot by Jesse Korman, it turns failed communication into a singalong with nobody else visibly present. Heard beside Faulty, the song makes the eventual question of solitude feel earned. Coming Home opens with Matthews in a smoky, Lynchian register, her voice suspended over steadily repeating synths and a breezy dance beat. The low guitar tones bring New Order to mind, with the melodic weight of a Peter Hook bassline translated onto guitar. That combination gives the song an appealing pull between bodily ease and emotional uncertainty. The rhythm leaves the windows open; the vocal suggests someone still deciding whether it is safe to come inside. Here, the album’s broader musical interests allow vulnerability to sound inviting without making it seem simple. Ice Pick (Walk Away) makes a particularly satisfying turn toward gothic rock. The parenthetical invites a Sisters of Mercy comparison before the guitar has even had its say, and the melody strengthens the association with their First and Last and Always period. A deep post-punk bass groove and the crunchy splash of the drum machine give the track a familiar dry ice chill. Matthews’ tender delivery moderates that severity, placing a vulnerable voice inside an arrangement with its collar firmly turned up. The resemblance is a pleasure to hear, especially from a duo whose love of this music has often been expressed through a different set of instruments. Pray 4 Me lets the bass loosen its hips. Soft synth pads, a sexy funk groove, and quivering bell tones bring a strain of Bryan Ferry-eque sophisti-pop into the album, expanding its capacity for pleasure as well as distress. There is a suppleness to the arrangement that makes this feel like a natural extension of the record’s emotional dynamic range. Desire, after all, does not become less complicated when somebody gives it a particularly good bassline. Boy Harsher sounds comfortable letting elegance and appetite share the same song. The album closes with Bleed, setting trip-hop beats against crystalline synths and low, bone-marrow-churning bass. Imagine the Bristol-born genre taking shape inside the electric dreams of the mid-1980s: the drums with a twitching hi-hat and thump have that low, unhurried weight, while the electronics give the space around them a cool, glassy clarity. After the movement of the preceding songs, this slower finish lets the record exhale. Its change of pace offers a place to sit with everything that has happened. Get Mean gives Matthews and Muller’s affection for post-punk, synthpop, goth, and dance music considerably more room to misbehave. They have grown as people, their lives have changed, and their music has had the good sense to evolve. Those expecting Pain on an endless loop, or Careful with a fresh set of track titles, may find this development inconvenient. For listeners who share Jae and Gus’s musical curiosity, there is pleasure in hearing them loosen up, follow their enthusiasms, and discover what this new chapter of their partnership can become. And if Get Mean isn’t the Boy Harsher you ordered, well, tough shit. Listen to Get Mean below and order the album here. Additional listening and purchase options are available here. GET MEAN by Boy Harsher Since forming in 2014, Matthews and Muller have taken Boy Harsher from the small cassette run of Lesser Man, whose Pain spread widely online, through Yr Body Is Nothing in 2016, the Country Girl EP in 2017, and Careful in 2019. items.body: Dudamel Conducts Prokofiev, Adams & Di Castri A visceral work headlined the opening program of the NY Philharmonic’s 2026-2027 season at Geffen Hall at Lincoln Center on September 16: John Adams’ On the Transmigration of Souls, a work written in response to the September 11 attacks on the World Trade Center. As the 25th anniversary of the tragedy was just a few days prior, my gut was still tender from the echoes of the memories of that day. The work included a recording on which the names of some of the victims were spoken. Even a quarter century later, hearing the names put me right into that somber feeling I had experienced last week. The work effectively conveyed the desperation, shock and numbness, grief and sadness of those days. In a way, the orchestra provided a soundtrack for this actuality, and the overall effect was mystical, otherworldly and deeply affecting. At the conclusion, an exceptionally long “hang time” of silence hung over the concert hall – even after conductor Gustavo Dudamel lowered his arms, a visual signal that the piece was over, the audience stayed quiet, giving a bit of contemplative quiet before the roaring applause. I didn’t feel like hearing anything else after that – I just wanted to go to a bar and have a stiff drink. I was curious how the next piece, a world premiere by Zosha Di Castri, would land directly after the emotional tension of the Adams piece. Di Castri’s Invisible House — co-commissioned by the Philharmonic — opened with low brass and bass, a rumble that I felt in my chest. The Philharmonic’s brass had a starring role here, and the entire section sounded brilliant. The piece felt a little unfocused, although that could have been me — my head was still occupied with the sounds and emotions of Transmigration of Souls. The program closed with Prokofiev’s Symphony No. 5, and on this more familiar ground it was apparent how utterly terrific the Philharmonic sounded. Timbres of the various orchestral sections blended beautifully – achieving a very well-balanced sound. The symphony’s dark undercurrent showed off the winds especially well. Gustavo Dudamel‘s energetic conducting style was entertaining to watch as his entire body twitched and convulsed in the bombastic sections. In this concert, the New York Philharmonic sounded as good, and as present, as I’ve ever heard them. Finally, four years after Geffen Hall’s renovation, the orchestra has settled into the hall, and the hall has wrapped itself around the orchestra. Both the band and the space have gotten used to each other and found ways to work together as a single organism. items.body: “Yira Ye” takes its title from a Bambara phrase that means roughly “that’s how it is”, and it is the first single from L’Ombre du Croco, the debut album  Bamako Express release through Trad Records on 30 October. The Ghent quartet pairs two Belgian folk players, violinist Anouk Sanczuk and guitarist Florian De Schepper, with Malian balafonist and singer Joël Massa Diarra and Burkinabè percussionist Ousmane Dembélé on djembe and calabash. Their songs are sung in Bambara. Over the past year they have played concert stages and the balfolk nights of Flanders, where couples dance to live folk bands, and in 2026 they won Best Live Band at the Flanders Folk Awards. At a balfolk night the violin carries the tune for the dancers, and in Mande music the balafon does much the same job; “Yira Ye” passes the melody between the two over Dembélé’s djembe. The track moves from quiet melodic passages into full dance rhythm, and De Schepper steps forward for a guitar solo, recorded with the rest of the song by Jeroen Geerinck at Studio Trad. items.body: All the things I’ve seen, all the things I’ve been must upset you. Moving to a new city after a broken heart requires a certain faith in geography. Surely a different address, unfamiliar faces, and a few hundred miles can improve upon the person who packed the suitcase. Then comes the stranger discovery: the life you once wanted has become difficult to remember. Berlin’s Pretty Average explores that uneasy freedom on All I Wanted, I Forgot, a song about starting over and finding that some of your most cherished desires have quietly missed the connection. That uncertainty carries into the accompanying video, where performance footage blurs beneath layers of static and bleeding color, matching the disorientation of the band’s beautiful blur of shoegaze, post-punk, and alternative rock. One of the earliest songs Pretty Average wrote together, All I Wanted, I Forgot appears on the album The Highs and Lows of Being Pretty Average, released on cassette this past May. A cascading drumbeat sets the song in motion while sustained guitar notes spread across a dense bed of distortion. The bass carries a melodic ache familiar from The Cure, giving the guitars something solid to stretch against. There is a sweet sadness here that recalls the distance and desolation of Joy Division, though the broadening shoegaze textures allow a softer, almost yielding quality into the music. Candy’s voice sits low in the mix, as though she is singing from the next room and leaving the door closed. That separation gives the words their peculiar weight. The lyrics inventory experiences, former selves, prayers, and departures, addressing someone who might resent everything that happened beyond their reach. By the time that accounting reaches “All I wanted, I forgot,” even the original wish has become elusive. As the guitars swell, their accumulating layers suggest water moving across an inscription, gradually making the names and promises harder to read. Forgetting carries its own small mercy, along with the disquiet of losing something you once thought essential. The band describes the song as an exploration of “the disturbing yet exciting feeling of being in a new city and starting over with a wounded heart, leaving behind your past and your dreams.” Their conclusion is brief enough to sound almost surprised: “Somehow we became someone new.” The video gives that uncertainty a physical form. Blue and violet stage lighting washes over the musicians while overlapping images, colour separation, and television static repeatedly interfere with the view. Faces and instruments become difficult to hold in focus; a close-up gives way to another image before either quite settles. The effect suggests a concert being recalled through an unreliable recording, with the band’s presence surviving all the visual interference. It suits a song in which the feeling remains clear even as its original object slips away. Watch the video for All I Wanted, I Forgot below: Formed in Berlin in 2022, Pretty Average centre Candy’s perspective on identity, social rejection, and the uncertain prospects facing her generation. Their 2024 EP, All I Wanted, was produced by Francisco Parisi of Minimal Schlager, with a Musicboard Berlin scholarship following that year. Regular Berlin performances, a Spanish tour, and support slots with acts including Genn, DVTR, Francis of Delirium, and Adult DVD helped develop a project whose priorities remain rooted in playing together. Those priorities took some recovering. Lineup difficulties and disagreements with their former label delayed an album originally intended for 2025; the band credits a European tour this May with renewing their enthusiasm. Recorded in a self-made studio, The Highs and Lows of Being Pretty Average preserves the energy and imperfections of musicians sharing a room. Its extended songs also reflect their stated preference for small venues, direct support, and giving an album room for long songs and changes of pace. The album is available on cassette through Bandcamp and at the band’s concerts. Listen to All I Wanted, I Forgot below and purchase the single here. The distinctive sound of the oud announces yet another musical tradition. Blending Mediterranean with Arabic sounds, the Lebanese-Belgian singer Amber Haddad and her trio, oudist Adil Benhsain and double bassist Martijn Vanbuel, spin a beguiling musical web. According to the liner notes (translated from the Dutch), �Tawazden� is about �seeking balance and finding peace within a complex environment.� Further, �the various spaces of the abbey and their murals are the direct source of inspiration.�
The accordion is especially prominent. So too is the Western classical tradition. Sounding almost Baroque, �Sacristia Invisibilis,� is another standout for me. Here, mandolinist Andries Boone is joined by Anouk Sanczuk on octave violin (sometimes called the baritone violin, tuned an octave lower than standard) and on harpsichord Sandra Van der Gucht. They create an indescribable sound you have to hear.
Throughout, the Abbey�s stone presence looms. Aur�lie Charneux�s solo clarinet piece �L'Ape Millenaria� is about a thousand-year-old bee that haunts the abbey. �Thila,� by Enara Navaira, evokes ancient Celts with a jazzy double bass and drum kit behind throat singing and Citera (a kind of Hungarian zither).

items.body: Editor's note: When this set of recordings came to me, I was at a loss as to how to share it. It's not music, in any traditional sense (although there is some freestyle rapping), and a 'review' of such an artifact of reality seems superfluous to the content. Instead, I asked sound recordist Ian Brennan if I could simply use his own brief commentary and the recordings he made on the street in Chicago. Twenty-five people afflicted by gun violence participated, many from the very block we�d setup on. Many neighbors were pulled-in spontaneously. Almost every one in the community had been impacted by violence somehow� both on the receiving and the inflicting end, and many both. One woman had just come from a memorial service, another was on her way. That�s how far-reaching the violence. Almost no one went untouched. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors By chance, we convened on the day that Trump ordered the deployment of the National Guard to the city. The recording took place on the front porch of the leader's ninety-four-year-old grandmother's house�right in the heart of the ��hood,� beneath the Midway Airport�s landing path. A pair of stray pitfalls stalked the block. But the grandmother warned not of gunshots, but the mosquitoes in her yard. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors We were in a section of town that one man defined as �the forgotten parts.� Just a short jaunt from the designer clothes shops and posh hotels of the city�s Magnificent Mile, the Southside spawned such legendary Blues artists as Muddy Waters, Willie Dixon, and Howlin� Wolf. Jazz musicians like Lionel Hampton and even Benny Goodman, hailed from nearby. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors The participants ranged in age from seventeen to sixty-seven, but the pattern held true. The person who�d asserted �you�ll really want to hear my story,� was the least compelling. The reluctant, the most moving. One elder�s tough facade broke down as she shared how she�d lost both her sons. She tearfully apologized, �I�m sorry. I�m sorry. I�m sorry.� But she had nothing to be sorry for. Society is the one that owes the apology� for the staggering statistical inequities of which no reasonable defense can be made. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors Editor's note: The full set of recordings are available on Bandcamp. Any profits from this project will be donated to Cure Violence Global , who states that their mission is "advancing an evidence-based health approach to end violence globally." When I asked him about the background sounds, producer Ian Brennan added, "No music is added. It�s all sounds from the source environment. I also ran loops/drones on a different track in the background as they spoke, and when they ended up being incidentally/somewhat magically/eerily synchronous, that is what was used for a few pieces with 'accompaniment' like some of the rap freestyles."

items.body: Amamere come from Cape Coast, the Fante fishing port where Ebo Taylor and C.K. Mann were born, and they play highlife the way Ghana’s guitar bands played it in the 1970s. Eric Asiedu Agyekum‘s lead guitar sits out front, tenor sax and trumpet play over the top, and behind the kit is Rim Akandoh Jnr, who spent the late 2010s drumming for Taylor. Their live take on “Kokonsani”, the opening track of the 2025 debut Man Shall Be Free on Afro Urban Project, was filmed at Afrika Festival Hertme in the Netherlands on 4 July, during the eight-piece’s first tour outside Ghana. Dominic Ansah plays Ga kpanlogo drums and congas under the kit, and the trumpet belongs to Emmanuel Adjei, grandson of Osibisa‘s Mac Tontoh. Akandoh Jnr’s father, Rim Akandoh, played in Mann’s band before leading the Prince Sparrows Band. Much of the album reworks his songs alongside osode, the fishing-community music Mann electrified, while “Kokonsani”, Twi for a gossip, carries the son’s own lyric. items.body: US goth-industrial artist EVA X released the single “Dance in Shadows” on 18 September 2026, alongside the announcement of her second album, “TURBOPINK”, due 6 November. The single mixes synthpop, metal, power pop and 80s-referencing production, and comes backed with a breakbeat remix by Stoneburner. “Dance in Shadows” was written by EVA X collaborator Gaby Gustafson after a co-worker and friend died of an aggressive form of cancer. “I had written a super sad song originally, but I knew she’d hate that. It was really important to her to find joy wherever she could. So I ended up reworking the track into Dance in Shadows, our happy little song about death,” Gustafson stated. The B-side carries a breakbeat remix of the track by Stoneburner. EVA X’s ‘TURBOPINK’ album due 6 November “TURBOPINK” follows EVA X’s debut album, “I Dream of a Reality”, released on Distortion Productions in 2022. “Dance in Shadows” serves as the album’s preview single. EVA X returns with a full band for the touring cycle around the new record. About EVA X EVA X began as a bedroom producer, releasing her first tracks in 2019 and building a following in the goth and industrial scene through a fusion of synthwave, industrial, power pop and metal elements. Her debut album, “I Dream of a Reality”, came out on Distortion Productions in 2022 and appeared on several “best of 2022” year-end lists. She has performed at New Jersey’s Dark Force Fest, Seattle’s Mechanismus Festival and Calgary’s Terminus. Side-Line previously covered her single and video “Dopamine Blind” (2024) and her video “Machine” (2021). With “Dance in Shadows”, EVA X previews her second album, “TURBOPINK”, out 6 November 2026.

items.body: US goth-pop project Metamorph released the single “Witchfire” and its official video on 18 September 2026. The track is produced by Erik Gustafson and pairs dance-oriented beats with hook-driven melodies, alongside an extended dance mix featuring a flute solo from vocalist Margot Day. The “Witchfire” video was filmed by Brian Wimer in New York’s East Village, where Margot Day lived and performed with The Plague in the 1980s, and in the forests of Vermont. It features Day alongside bandmate Kurtis Knight. The extended dance mix, which includes Day’s flute solo, will get its own video at a later date. Metamorph’s release history Metamorph is the project of Margot Day, a New York vocalist, flutist and songwriter who fronted The Plague during the 1980s NYC goth scene alongside drummers Nick Ferrell (Spahn Ranch) and Damian (Misfits). Earlier in her career, Day played in Slow Walk 13 alongside Adam Yauch of the Beastie Boys. Formed in 2016, Metamorph blends gothic atmosphere, dark synth textures and pop songwriting built around Day’s vocals and flute playing, with Kurtis Knight providing dark synths and backing vocals on stage. Metamorph’s back catalogue includes the album “Kiss of the Witch” (2022), the album “Hex” (2024) and the retrospective “Haunted Hearts XIII” (2025), all produced by Erik Gustafson. The project has released remixes by Leaether Strip and Assemblage 23, and the single “Dance of a 1000 Miracles” featuring Stabbing Westward‘s Chris Hall has passed 20,000 Spotify streams. Metamorph has performed across the United States, Canada, Costa Rica and Guatemala, with music videos totalling more than 250,000 YouTube views. “Witchfire” follows Metamorph’s 2025 EP “Harlot” on Distortion Productions.

items.body: Ghost Reflection, the dark electro and industrial project of Alexander Borsov, releases the concept album “Dark Triad” digitally on Aliens Production. The eight-track record mixes melodic lines, IDM loops and analog electronics around a horror-themed narrative. Borsov wrote, produced, designed and mastered “Dark Triad” himself. Aliens Production describes the record as “a cinematic concept rooted in horror aesthetics and rhythmic themes.” The tracklist runs “Games of psychopaths,” “Dark Triad,” “Integration of Madness,” “Infected,” “The root of evil,” “Thorny path,” “The Shattered World of Illusions” and “Order of Darkness.” Dark Triad by Ghost Reflection Ghost Reflection’s ‘Dark Triad’ concept The eight tracks move from “Games of psychopaths” through “Integration of Madness” and “The root of evil” to the closing “Order of Darkness,” a sequence built around horror imagery and rhythmic industrial and IDM production rather than a conventional song structure. “Dark Triad” first appeared under Borsov’s own Bandcamp page in September 2025 and now returns through Aliens Production as a digital release. About Ghost Reflection Ghost Reflection is one of several recording names used by Slovak producer Alexander Borsov, alongside Dark the Keeper, Darkmechanic and Stellar Dynamics, all mixing electro-industrial, noise and horror-themed dark electro elements. Borsov is also a member of the group Diverje and got his start in metal bands including Morgue, Atom, Cremation Deads, Sarcoma and Satura before moving into electronic production. Under the Ghost Reflection name, Borsov released the album “Dark Thinker” in June 2022 and the single “Dark Noise” in February 2024. “Dark Triad” followed in September 2025 and is now released digitally through Aliens Production, the Slovak dark electronics label that has operated since 1997 and hosts a roster of industrial, dark electro and EBM-adjacent acts.

The album, with its stage show and book, tells the story of the garden�s oldest specimen, a Sabal palm tree ( Sabal bermudana ), which was gently felled in 2021, and contained a surprise nobody had expected. The tree is the starting point. From there, imagination runs free. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan It�s an album of voice and piano (the outstanding, sympathetic Dave Milligan), and, for all its global outlook on connections, one that�s very rooted in Scotland. You can hear it on the opening track, �Hear The Rigging/Last In Line,� where the melody becomes a slow, aching lament that would sound completely natural on the pipes. The stripped-down sound gives the songs both crafted stateliness and real intimacy. Each one is an exhalation, a memory, a celebration and exploration, with recurring phrases in the words and music acting as touchstones � or even hooks; they certainly stick in the mind. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan In many ways, this is a modest album, with piano, voice and light, judicious soundscaping. It won�t overpower with noise. Yet at the same time, it�s epic, a look at history, at the flow and grandeur of nature, and the things we all carry within us. The music, and especially Polwart�s warm, compassionate voice, envelop the listener, and makes them a participant, not an observer, but a part of the journey and the history. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan The irony arrives at the end, when the venerable old tree is down, and seeds are examined. What people for two hundred years had believed to be a Sabal bermudana turns out to be something different, a Sabal mexicana � and one of the small plants fill grow where it�s forerunner once stood. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan Like music, plants keep to a different time � and this album/book/show give the tree the requiem it deserves, as well as hope for the future. items.body:
According to its founder, Eugene Rodriguez, who also sings and plays on the record, Los Cenzontles is a �musical group and non-profit organization, which I founded over thirty years ago.�  As he continues in the album�s liner notes, the group �has a long history of producing projects exploring Mexico�s deep roots and our connections with various traditions that, so far, have included Irish, Louisiana Creole, Cuban, American cowboy, classical, pop, rock, and blues�, the latest of which is
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
. Los Cenzontles translates to the mockingbird, or, from its Aztec root word, the bird of four hundred voices. This is a fitting name for the range of musical diversity represented here.
With songs sung in Spanish, Hawaiian, and English, the concept traces back to the legacy of Mexican cowboys who travelled from California to the Hawaiian Islands to wrangle the long-horned cattle introduced there in the nineteenth century. They also brought the guitar. The 16 tracks feature old Hawaiian songs with new Spanish lyrics, old Mexican songs with new Hawaiian lyrics, new compositions, and traditional Americana. Yet it is an entirely cohesive musical package held together by dense arrangements of ukuleles, guitars, Mexican harp, and accordion.
Sonny Lim & David Hidalgo
Besides their distinctive voices, the headline artists Taj Mahal and David Hidalgo provide the gravitas and musicianship that their long and distinguished careers have earned. According to the liner notes, they were the catalysts behind the project and facilitated the choice of songs, arrangements, and played a range of instruments. On vocals they are joined by Hawaiian natives Gary Haleamau, Sheldeen Haleamau, Sonny Lim, and long-time Cenzontles member Fabiola Trujillo.
Deportee
To give a taste of the sessions, included before the traditional �Fishin� Blues� is Taj Mahal teaching the musicians how to play it. Sung by David Hildalgo,  the lovely �A Matter of Time� comes from the 1984 album
Will the Wolf Survive
by his most famous project, Los Lobos. Another standout for me, �Navegar� features a slack string guitar solo reminiscent of Duane Eddie and one of many tasty lap steel turns by Sonny Lim. Their interpretation of Woody Guthrie's �Deportee� moves into social commentary, highlighting the cruel realities of being a migrant worker in America.
Vaquero Paniolo
Recorded over five days, mostly live in one room at the Los Cenzontles headquarters in San Pablo, California, including the talents of some of their academy�s students, the recording has real spontaneity to it. Arrangements are stretched by improvisations, sometimes by several different instruments on a single tune. The project also represents a great spirit of cooperation and diversity of language, culture, age, and gender. It includes the inputs of musical legends, seasoned pros, and amateurs. The wonderfully rich and often stereotyped musical cultures of both Mexico and Hawaii are represented here with the authenticity of lived experience.
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
is a worthy addition to Los Cenzontles� important work. Quoting Rodriguez again, �Culture is a fabric within which we are all woven.�

The musical partnership between Kalaniemi and Alakotila has thrived over a remarkable 35 years, long enough to the Finnish pair to develop a stunning intimacy and telepathy. Kalaniemi is a lovingly melodic accordion player, with a sharp ear for a good tune, building each one into a thing of great beauty, while pianist Alakotila not only supports her but adds enough of his own to help transform every piece into a glistening gem.
There�s a sense of calmness to the work here, a long, sweet exhalation between two instrumentalists who are deep enough in sync to allow seamless improvisation beyond any written score and carry the listeners along with them. For much of the album, it�s just the pair of them, including Kalaniemi�s wordless voice, as on the opener, the tradional �Lyck�nskan.� She does charmingly sing lyrics on the title track, written by Lasse M�rtenson, with the sound there neatly and sparingly expanded with the addition of a string quartet.
Morgondimma
There are several original pieces alongside the tradition, with Kalaniemi�s �Hambo Vid F�bodan� a real standout, and it�s perhaps inevitable on any disc featuring accordion that a Piazzolla tune should be included, brings its own shadows to the whole (�Oblivion�). And, this being Finland, a tango is almost obligatory, in this case Alakotila�s �Tango Berlin.�
Tango Berlin
There�s a gentle, dreamlike quality to so much of this, flowing and mellifluous. The pieces aren�t an arena for showy virtuosity. Instead, the two musicians serve the tune, exploring and genuinely enjoying their performances.
It won�t shake the earth, but it makes for some true listening beauty.

items.body:
Sometime in 1986, perhaps in a Paris caf�, Dominique Cravic, a singer, guitarist, and musical archivist, met Robert Crumb, an underground cartoonist, banjo and mandolin player, and jug-band aficionado. Over a few glasses of marc, to continue to speculate, they conjured up the idea for Les Primitifs du futur.  Since then, they have recorded an impossible-to-categorize series of albums, with cover illustrations by Crumb, of which Les Crimes du Mussette is the fifth.
Weird and wonderful, it sounds like they rooted through an attic full of 78 RPM records, scribbled down some arrangements, and then played them on a collection of instruments they found in another attic, including accordion, sax, xylophone, clarinet, banjo, ukulele, theremin, Hawaiian guitar, bagpipe chanter (I�m guessing here), and musical saw.
Ne tirez pas sur le pianiste (excerpt)
The 27 short tracks are mostly voiced by Cravic, who talk-sings in the manner of an everyman Maurice Chevalier. He is often accompanied by the accordion, a customary instrument in the bal-musette style that remains a strong element of the eclectic range of styles they have managed to synthesize. They also include ragtime, jug, French chanson, and, to my ears, skiffle,  just to get the list started.
Ukulele Lady (excerpt)
The liner notes point out that �Les Crimes du Musette is also a gold mine for scholars, a veritable treasure trove.� Exploring the treasures is beyond my scope here, as each tune has a long history. A highlight for me is the humorous �Ukulele Lady� from 1925, which first delighted me on Arlo Guthrie�s 1971 album
Hobo�s Lullaby
. The song has also been covered by Bing Crosby, Peter Sellers, and Bette Midler.
N'oublie pas Gr�co (excerpt)
A more serious item is �N�oublie pas Gr�co� (Don�t Forget Gr�co�)  is a tribute to the legendary chanteuse and heroine of the French Resistance, Juliette Gr�co, who died in 2020. You will also hear old chestnuts like �Fum�e aux yeux� (�Smoke Gets in Your Eyes�),  �Boude pas� (�Take Five�), and �Prive d�amour� (�As Time Goes By�).
This record is a curiosity, but it is performed by serious musicians with total commitment. In this, I was reminded of the similarly indefinable Dan Hicks & the Hot Licks. Long-forgotten music and abandoned styles are given new animation with obvious enthusiasm and care. Speaking about himself and his collaborators, many of whom are in their seventies, Dominique Cravic says, �The young have fire, but we have light.� In its own little corner,
Les Crimes du Musette
shines bright.

items.body: Ska and rocksteady set the tempo on “Be Who You Are”, a faster footing than the roots rhythms Macka B ordinarily records over, and he toasts across it in the measured address that has defined his delivery since the early 1980s. The single was released on 21 August, composed and produced by the Hamburg musician Paul Lupa, who plays keyboards and bass and surrounds them with a live rhythm section: Big Finga on drums, Robert “Dubwise” Browne on guitar, Tribuman on horns. The horns carry the melodic line, the guitar marks the offbeat, and the vocal sits forward in the mix, with the phrasing of a lyric Macka B wrote himself, vocal melody included. What he tells the listener is to be who they are. Advice has been his line of work for forty years. He has been called “the Teacher” since the 1980s for songs about what to eat, how to look after yourself and how to treat other people, and the Wha Me Eat Wednesdays vegan raps he began posting in 2017 carried that voice far beyond the reggae circuit. Lupa has been building his Hamburg catalogue around Jamaican and German vocalists since 2022, and Macka B is the most established voice to record over one of his rhythms so far. items.body: Cocteau Twins released their fifth studio album, “Blue Bell Knoll,” through 4AD on 19 September 1988. Capitol Records licensed the record from 4AD for North America, making it the first Cocteau Twins album to receive major-label distribution in the United States. The dream pop album turns 38 this year. Vocalist Elizabeth Fraser named the album after Bluebell Knoll, a peak in southern Utah. Guitarist Robin Guthrie produced the record and handled keyboards along with synth and drum machine programming, while Simon Raymonde played bass and keyboards. All ten tracks are credited to Fraser, Guthrie and Raymonde: the title track, “Athol-Brose,” “Carolyn’s Fingers,” “For Phoebe Still a Baby,” “The Itchy Glowbo Blow,” “Cico Buff,” “Suckling the Mender,” “Spooning Good Singing Gum,” “A Kissed Out Red Floatboat” and “Ella Megalast Burls Forever.” Fraser sang the whole album in her own constructed language. Raymonde later described the sessions as a settled period for the trio: “it really felt like a period of creativity and freedom, we were all getting on great musically and socially, Liz and Robin were about to have a baby, I was about to get married, there was lots of joy around. Very productive! It was a really fun record to make.” Fraser connected that ease to the decision to drop conventional lyrics, telling The Quietus in 2017: “I gained so much from [inventing language] […] Writing Blue Bell Knoll I had a wonderful freedom to put lyrics aside and not to worry [about people’s opinions].” The album reached number 15 on the UK Albums Chart and number 109 on the US Billboard 200, and “Carolyn’s Fingers” climbed to number two on the US Alternative Airplay chart. Promotional videos accompanied “Carolyn’s Fingers” and “Cico Buff.” The vinyl edition came in a limited gatefold sleeve, and the album was the first 4AD title issued commercially on DAT. After 4AD reclaimed the North American rights to its back catalogue, Guthrie remastered “Blue Bell Knoll” for a 2003 reissue, and the album was repressed on 180g vinyl in 2014. It streams on Spotify. About Cocteau Twins Cocteau Twins formed in 1979 in Grangemouth, Scotland, around guitarist Robin Guthrie and bassist Will Heggie, who took the band name from a song by fellow Scots Simple Minds. Guthrie met Elizabeth Fraser in Falkirk in 1981 and asked her to sing. The group signed to 4AD and issued its debut album, “Garlands,” in 1982, followed by “Head over Heels” in 1983. Heggie left that year and Simon Raymonde replaced him, arriving in time for 1984’s “Treasure.” Two albums came in 1986: “Victorialand,” recorded largely as a duo while Raymonde worked on This Mortal Coil, and “The Moon and the Melodies,” a collaboration with ambient composer Harold Budd. “Blue Bell Knoll” followed on 19 September 1988 and became the band’s first record to enter the US Billboard 200, a direct result of the Capitol licensing deal. “Heaven or Las Vegas” arrived in 1990 and closed the group’s run on 4AD; Cocteau Twins then signed to Fontana for “Four-Calendar Café” (1993) and “Milk & Kisses” (1996), and disbanded in 1997. All three have kept working since. Side-Line covered Raymonde’s Bella Union label presenting the debut album by his project Lost Horizons in 2017, Guthrie’s ‘Riviera’ EP in 2021 and his ‘Springtime’ EP in 2022, and reported that Fraser had returned with her first new material in 13 years in 2022. “Blue Bell Knoll” turns 38 this year, the record that opened the American market to the band two years before its 4AD run ended.
